scams.name: 'Costa Joe' — Named WhatsApp/Facebook Fixer Deposit Fraud (Cars, Golf Carts, Airbnbs)
scams.description:
Community reports warn about the most-named individual scammer operating against Jacó-bound tourists. Travelers describe the pattern: 'there is a guy that calls himself Costa Joe or other variations, particularly on FB. He sets up other varying profiles and uses those profiles to act as a reference. He will pretend to get you set with car, car rentals, Airbnbs, rides, golf carts, and anything else he can promise and try to get you to pay a deposit. Then when it's time to deliver, he ghosts. Been scamming for quite a while. He's probably early to mid-20's, WhatsApp is his preferred method of communication.' The Facebook 'Playas del Coco' group post 'Scam Alert: Beware of Joseph Goodwin and Costa Joe in Car Deals' confirms the real name and extends the racket to Coco/Guanacaste. Named-victim testimony includes: 'Joseph Goodwin. He sold me a messed up car claiming all good. Looks like I got lucky since I actually got a car, another lady paid and got ghosted'; 'Yes, Costa Joe is well known on some Facebook groups. Many people have been ripped off by him'; 'Already reported his number as a scam in TrueCaller.' The racket is classic advance-fee: a $200–$800 USD deposit via SINPE Móvil, WhatsApp-linked transfer, Zelle, or crypto for a car rental, golf cart, Airbnb, fishing charter, or jetski; after payment the address produces no car and no answer. Sock-puppet FB accounts tag each other with fake 'great guy, rented from him twice' endorsements to build social proof.

For travelers planning a Jacó rental in 2025/2026, the playbook: (1) book cars only through major chains — Adobe Rent-a-Car, Budget, Economy, Alamo, National — at SJO airport pickup in person; never WhatsApp handoff; average $45–$100/day with insurance disclosed at counter; (2) golf carts: rent only at physical Avenida Pastor Díaz storefronts (JacoLuxe, AXR Jaco, Adventure Tours CR) — never from Facebook; 2025 rates $80–$120/day, deposits $200–$300 on card; (3) refuse all WhatsApp/Facebook deposit requests from individuals, even if 'recommended' — sock puppets are the mechanism; (4) Airbnbs only through Airbnb platform payment — never 'partly cash on arrival' or 'Zelle me a deposit'; (5) fishing/jetski: licensed ICT-registered operators only (Pacific Jungle Adventures, Maverick Sportfishing, R Sport Fishing); (6) if you've paid Costa Joe, email OIJ fraud (oij_fraudes@poder-judicial.go.cr), file credit-card chargeback within 60 days; travelers also recommend contacting Trivision, Central Noticias, or Multimedios 'to put pressure on the bureaucrats to do something.'
scams.avoidance: Cars: only major chains at SJO counter (Adobe, Budget, Alamo, National, Economy). Golf carts: Avenida Pastor Díaz physical storefronts (JacoLuxe, AXR Jaco) — card deposit. Airbnbs: Airbnb platform payment only — refuse any 'cash on arrival' request. Charters/jetski: licensed ICT-registered operators (Pacific Jungle Adventures, Maverick, R Sport Fishing). If scammed: OIJ fraud email oij_fraudes@poder-judicial.go.cr + credit-card chargeback within 60 days.

scams.name: Jacó Beach Parking Fake 'No-Park Zone' Reflective-Vest Extortion
scams.description:
Travelers describe the mechanism: 'If you are parking in Jaco beach area there is a scam there where they will rope your car off and say you parked in a no park zone when you didn't. They wear a reflective vest and it all seems real … they'll ask for a random amount of $.' The scam exploits Costa Rica's informal 'guachiman' (from English 'watchman') culture where unofficial attendants legitimately work Jacó beach lots in yellow vests and expect a ₡500–₡2,000 (~$1–$4) tip. The scam inverts it: men in identical vests rope off a legal spot with cones or caution tape, wait for a tourist to park, then demand '$20 or I call the tow truck.' Community reports extend the pattern to organized break-ins at the Jaco Walk plaza lot specifically — 'the parking guard was in on it': the 'attendant' is casing the vehicle and signaling accomplices with an RF key-jammer that blocks the fob lock signal so your car flashes but doesn't lock. Travelers also flagged the vehicle-specific pattern: 'The jimny car seems like the main target for this type of robbery, they know its a rental car and tourists often travel with all of their belongings in the car.' Coordination has been reported at Jaco Walk, Hotel Cocal lot, and the main Playa Jacó beach strip.

For travelers parking in Jacó in 2025/2026, the playbook: (1) use hotel or restaurant parking over street parking — Jaco Walk interior, Crocs Resort lot, and Los Sueños marina lots have CCTV; (2) if you must street-park, legitimate guachimen accept ₡500–₡1,000 (~$1–$2) tip on return — anyone demanding $10–$20 upfront is running the scam; (3) never pay a 'fine' in cash to a reflective-vested man claiming a no-park zone — demand municipal paperwork (Boleta Municipal de Tránsito, stamped); (4) double-check your car is actually locked after the fob press — pull the handle manually; the key-jammer trick is widespread at Central Pacific beach lots; (5) never leave passports, laptops, cameras, or daypacks visible — hide them in the trunk before arriving at the lot (thieves watch the transfer); (6) if extorted or threatened, note the vest number, photograph the scene, and report to Jacó Tourist Police substation or OIJ Jacó subdelegación on Avenida Pastor Díaz, or call 911 (English dispatch via the new Tourist Police Operations Center, launched Sept 2025).
scams.avoidance: Park at hotel/restaurant lots with CCTV (Jaco Walk interior, Crocs Resort, Los Sueños). Legitimate guachiman tip: ₡500–₡1,000 on return — never a fixed dollar amount upfront. Pull the door handle manually after locking — defeat key-jammer trick. Hide all valuables in trunk before arriving at the lot (never during transfer). Report extortion: OIJ Jacó subdelegación Avenida Pastor Díaz, or call 911.

scams.name: Monteverde/Jacó Tours CR Copycat-Domain Booking Fraud
scams.description:
Community reports document the SEO-based copycat-domain fraud that has been draining deposits from Jacó- and Monteverde-bound travelers since at least 2023. One traveler put a dollar figure on the monteverdetourscr.com copycat: 'Our travel group booked a tour with monteverdetourscr.com in May paying $1000 USD for 4 people. The tour date was scheduled for August 28, 2024. The day before we were notified the tour was cancelled and given an alternate date, that we could not make. The company said they would process a refund. Here we are in November and after about 35 emails, whatsapp communications and the run-around, we still haven't received a refund.' Another traveler noted: 'When this company started they directly copied the name of well known respected company called Monteverde Tours (the only change was they added CR to their email).' The legitimate company is monteverdetours.com (since 2002); the scam is monteverdetourscr.com. The same domain farm books Jacó-side day-tours (Carara crocodile boat, Catarata Bijagual, Jacó zipline combos). One traveler wrote: 'They canceled the tour because the water levels were too high. 2 months now, they've promised to refund me. Going through CapitalOne to get my money back.' Scamwatcher.com (823633) lists WhatsApp +506 7114-7550 as flagged; the TripAdvisor review page (d14145312 review 970744950) is titled 'FRAUD DO NOT BOOK.' Travelers name the tell: 'one thing that's a red flag on their site is they don't link you to any review sites like tripadvisor or get your guide or viator.' Another adds: 'never put that size of a deposit down, ever... maybe $50–$100. Always pay on arrival.'

For travelers booking Jacó-area tours in 2025/2026, the playbook: (1) never prepay more than a $50–$100 deposit — legitimate operators (Jacó Tours, Adventure Tours CR, Pacific Jungle Adventures) accept balance on arrival in cash or card; (2) book through buyer-protected marketplaces — Viator, GetYourGuide, Expedia Tours, or TripAdvisor Experiences — which refund when operators cancel; (3) verify the operator's TripAdvisor listing before paying; if no TripAdvisor/Viator link on the operator's own site, that's the red flag; (4) pay credit card only (Visa/Mastercard) — never wire, SINPE, Zelle, crypto; chargeback via issuer is the only reliable recovery (travelers report money came back via Chase fraud investigation); (5) cross-reference on Google — monteverdetours.com (since 2002) vs monteverdetourscr.com (scam); similar copycats exist for 'Jaco Tours' and 'Arenal Tours'; (6) if scammed, file credit-card dispute within 60 days and report to Defensoría del Consumidor at consumidor.go.cr.

scams.name: SJO↔Jacó 'Private Shuttle' & Taxi Overcharge at Arrivals
scams.description:
Jacó sits 96 km (1 hr 45 min) southwest of SJO on Route 27, and the transfer is the most over-quoted tourist run in Costa Rica. Community reports establish the 2024/2025 baseline: 'Taxi is around $120. Pura vida rides advertises $109 (WhatsApp +506 7189-3268). I've heard didi is cheaper.' Travelers confirm: '$70, from downtown, on a Monday morning. No issues' and '$140 is pretty normal for a private shuttle to Jaco. You could probably get an uber slightly cheaper if there are fewer than 3 in your party.' The budget option: San Jose–Jaco public bus at $6–$8 cash, every 2 hours from downtown Terminal 7-10 (not the airport — a short Uber from SJO). The scam: tourists at SJO arrivals are approached by men waving 'Shuttle Jacó' signs quoting $200–$300 for a run that legitimately costs $120 by metered taxi, $70–$100 Uber/DiDi, or $50–$65/person via Interbus shared shuttle. Related: unverified 'driver' numbers from Facebook groups demand USD prepayment via Zelle/Venmo, then either no-show or demand second cash payment claiming the prepayment 'didn't go through.' One traveler noted: 'My Airbnb hosts in San Jose offered me rides that were 40 to 133 percent more than Uber.' Another long-time resident summarized: 'as someone who had been a resident of Costa Rica for 17 years, taxi drivers will always try to charge you excessive fares specially.'

scams.name: Jacó ATV & Golf Cart Rental Damage-Inflation Deposit Trap
scams.description:
Jacó is Costa Rica's ATV and golf-cart rental capital, with legitimate and scam operators side-by-side on Avenida Pastor Díaz. 2025/2026 prices at reputable storefronts (AXR Jaco, Adventure Tours CR, Aventuras AVT Rentals, JacoLuxe): ATV 2-hour ~$90, half-day (4h) $150, full-day (8h) $200, 24-hour $250; golf cart $80–$120/day with $200–$300 credit-card-hold. One traveler noted: 'Our car rental deposit was released within 24 hours. The ATV deposit took almost a week. It wasn't a big deal...' — delayed releases are the norm, not the scam. The scam comes from two sides: (1) Costa-Joe WhatsApp fixers demanding cash deposits for a 'golf cart that will be delivered'; (2) Front-office damage-inflation — the vehicle passes pre-rental with only generic scratches noted, then on return staff 'discovers' a new scratch, 'cracked fender,' 'worn tires,' or 'mud damage' and bills $300–$800. Community reports note: 'How did u guys pay the deposit? These are the payment options I got from them on whatsapp and none seem a good option' — sketchy operators request SINPE Móvil transfers to personal accounts rather than card at the counter. Travelers catalog the pattern: 'lowball car rentals are the bait, and high insurance or $2700 to $20000 deposits if [damage found].' The pattern extends to Jacó ATVs/golf carts — smaller deposit, same inflation tactic.

For travelers renting ATVs or golf carts in Jacó in 2025/2026, the playbook: (1) rent only from Avenida Pastor Díaz storefronts with Google Maps presence — AXR Jaco, Aventuras AVT Rentals, JacoLuxe, Adventure Tours CR; never from WhatsApp-only 'fixers'; (2) pre-rental walkaround is non-negotiable — take a date-stamped 360° video (not photos) including tires, fender undersides, engine compartment BEFORE leaving the lot; narrate defects into the mic; save to cloud; (3) inspection sheet must list EVERY existing defect before you sign — if they refuse or list 'general scratches,' walk away; (4) pay deposit by credit card (Visa/Mastercard) — never cash or SINPE Móvil — so you have chargeback power; a $200–$300 card hold is legitimate, a $500+ cash demand is not; (5) 2025 rates: ATV $90/2hr, $150 half-day, $200 full-day, $250 24hr; golf cart $80–$120/day with $200–$300 card hold; anything far below is bait; (6) at return, joint walkaround + fresh video; refuse to sign 'damage acknowledged' without seeing pre-rental video; dispute fraudulent charges via card and Defensoría del Consumidor (consumidor.go.cr).
scams.avoidance: Rent only from Avenida Pastor Díaz storefronts: AXR Jaco, Aventuras AVT, JacoLuxe, Adventure Tours CR. Deposit by credit card (card hold $200–$300) — never cash or SINPE. Return: joint walkaround + fresh video; dispute any fabricated damage via card issuer.

scams.name: Jacó Mirador & Beach Opportunistic Robbery / Belongings Theft
scams.description:
The Mirador Jacó (abandoned villa viewpoint above south Jacó with graffiti and Pacific views) is the most-named specific robbery hotspot in Jacó. One traveler wrote: 'Stay away from the Mirador Jaco - tourists get robbed there all day, every day.' Counter-voices report uneventful midday visits — the risk cluster is late afternoon, evening, solo walkers, and visible camera gear. Combined with beach theft on Playa Jacó, travelers report: 'unattended phones and wallets disappear quickly.' Community reports surface adjacent Playa Hermosa beach-parking theft: 'Yep same thing happened to my Jimny earlier this month near Uvita' with passenger door pried and iPhone gone. Another traveler summarized: 'Property crime is the biggest issue in CR for visitors. Car break-ins, AirBnB burglaries, theft of belongings left unattended on the beach.' The Tico Times 'Danger in Costa Rica? Rising Crime' names Jacó; travelers add: 'Tamarindo has become Jacó but more expensive. Thanks to the drug market.' The Jacó beach pattern: a tourist leaves phone/wallet/daypack on a towel; a walker lifts the bag while they're 30m offshore; the walker blends into Avenida Pastor Díaz within 90 seconds. Mirador variant: 2–3 men approach a solo hiker near the villa, ask for the time/directions, demand phone and wallet.

For travelers at Jacó beaches and the Mirador in 2025/2026, the playbook: (1) never hike the Mirador Jacó solo — groups of 3+, daylight only, before 4 PM; the trail is short (~30 min up) but the isolated villa area is where approaches happen; (2) on Playa Jacó, carry only what fits in a waterproof neck-pouch (phone, one card, $20 cash, hotel key) — everything else in the hotel safe; (3) use a dry-bag phone pouch in the water rather than a towel on sand; (4) at Playa Hermosa surf break (5 km south), park at Backyard Bar/Hotel lot ($5 attended) rather than roadside — surf-bag theft at roadside is documented; (5) after sunset do NOT walk the beach — risk ranking: beach-at-night > Mirador > parking-lot > Avenida Pastor Díaz > hotel-room; travelers note: 'The risk on beaches at night is robbery and theft'; (6) if robbed: no resistance, hand items over, walk to a lit restaurant, call 911 (new 2025 Tourist Police Operations Center with English dispatch); report to OIJ Jacó subdelegación on Avenida Pastor Díaz within 24h for insurance claim.
scams.avoidance: Mirador Jacó: groups of 3+, daylight only, never after 4 PM. Beach: waterproof neck-pouch for phone/card/$20/key — rest in hotel safe. Playa Hermosa: park at attended Backyard Bar/Hotel lot ($5), never roadside. Never walk Jacó beach after sunset — beach-at-night is the top risk. If robbed: no resistance, call 911, OIJ Jacó on Avenida Pastor Díaz within 24h.

scams.name: Fake/Unlicensed 'Certified Guide' Ambush at Monteverde Cloud Forest Reserve Gate
scams.description:
Since December 2024, Monteverde Cloud Forest Reserve has required online timed-entry at $29 USD per adult per circuit (three circuits: Sendero Bosque Nuboso, Sendero Pantanoso, Sendero Chomogo) with caps per slot — the Tico Times 2026 'Monteverde Reserve Caps Daily Visitors with Online Timed Entry System' and community reports both confirm. Travelers note: 'Before, people could buy a day pass at the door and stay as long as you wanted. Now, they offer entrance fees to 3 separate trail circuits, and you must purchase an entrance pass per trail beforehand.' The ambush scam exploits the new system's confusion: unlicensed 'certified guide' operators intercept tourists on the approach road or in the parking lot before the gate, claiming the reserve is 'sold out' or 'you need a guide today' or 'I have special access to Curi-Cancha/Santa Elena which is better,' then charge $50–$100 for an unguided walk at a different property. One traveler wrote: 'I had arranged a tour at Monteverde Cloud Forest and heard from the people I thought I had arranged it with that they couldn't do the Cloud Forest but offered me CuriCancho instead... I feel like I'm in the middle of a turf war or a scam.' Another added: 'people have bought tickets only to be told they have to wait for hours before they can do the tour.' A TripAdvisor review (942706612, 'Scam - Roy's the Monteverde local nature guide') states: 'Big time scam. They rob you blind. Do not go. You have to buy your own ticket after you pay this scammer.' Legitimate ICT-certified guides hold laminated credentials with photo and ICT registration number, cross-referenced at visitcostarica.com's guide directory.

For travelers at the Monteverde or Santa Elena reserves in 2025/2026, the playbook: (1) buy timed-entry ONLY at cloudforestmonteverde.com — $29/adult/circuit, book 3–7 days ahead in Dec–April high season; save PDF offline; (2) Santa Elena Reserve: $18 foreign adult / $9 child (8–12) via reservasantaelena.org — not sold at the gate by strangers; (3) for a guide, hire through hotel concierge (Hotel Belmar, Hidden Canopy Treehouses, Senda Monteverde vet local guides) or pre-book via Viator/GetYourGuide — never from a man flagging you down on the road; (4) verify the guide's ICT laminated certification (photo + registration number) — ask and photograph it before paying; (5) 2025/2026 guided prices: $35–$45 guided walk + $29 reserve entry at Monteverde; private 3-hour Santa Elena walk $65 via Viator; refuse any 'all-in $80–$100 guide + entry' at the gate — the math doesn't work at legitimate rates; (6) Curi-Cancha Reserve IS a legitimate bird/wildlife reserve (Resplendent Quetzal sightings confirmed) but is NOT the Monteverde Cloud Forest — gate intercepts pushing Curi-Cancha as 'better' are selling a bait-and-switch; book both separately if you want both.

scams.name: Monteverde 'Hostel Desk' Commission Overcharge on Tour Bookings (Night Walks, Zipline, Coffee Tours)
scams.description:
Santa Elena/Monteverde's compact village (one main road with 60+ tour operators, hostels, and kiosks) runs a commission-overlay ecosystem that starts as convenience and slides into scam when markup crosses 30% or quality drops. One traveler wrote: 'Went on a jungle night walk in Monteverde. It felt VERY set up, like a farm or zoo, not authentic wildlife. It was a maze-like forest where guides had walkie-talkies to tell each other where animals were.' Another added: 'People say they feed some animals with dog food to keep them around, so it kinda is a setup.' Scam variants: (1) hostel desk books a 'night walk for $50' that legit costs $30–$40 at the operator (Monteverde Travel's night tour $40, Viator Small Group Night Walk $38), pocketing $10–$15 markup; (2) 'sold-out-but-my-cousin-has-slots' pitch where a 'cousin' runs an unlicensed operation on a private farm trail; (3) 'coffee tour $90 package' that legitimately costs $52 at Don Juan Tours direct (donjuantoursmonteverde.com) or $40–$64 via Viator; (4) Selvatura Park zipline 'package' at $120 when direct is $80 adult + 13% tax (selvatura.com). Another traveler reports: 'more tour guides who shared their low monthly earnings at the end to encourage you to tip, after already paying the $80–150 tour cost.' Community reports confirm legitimate prices — one traveler: 'We did the nightwalk with a private guide, Felix (WhatsApp 506-8706-5456), at the Wildlife Refuge in MonteVerde.'

For travelers in Santa Elena/Monteverde in 2025/2026, the playbook: (1) know the legitimate direct 2025/2026 rates: Selvatura zipline $80 + tax; Selvatura combo ~$90 (Viator 2026); Monteverde Cloud Forest entry $29/circuit; Santa Elena Reserve entry $18; Don Juan Coffee/Chocolate/Sugarcane $52 direct ($40–$64 Viator); Monteverde Night Walk $38–$40; 100% Aventura zipline ~$90; (2) book direct from operator websites — cloudforestmonteverde.com, reservasantaelena.org, selvatura.com, donjuantoursmonteverde.com — to lock the no-markup price; (3) Viator/GetYourGuide tour bookings typically include pickup at major Santa Elena hotels at no extra charge; (4) if you prefer hostel desk convenience, ALWAYS ask 'What is this same tour at the operator's website?' — legitimate hostels (Pensión Santa Elena, Camino Verde) run honest 10–15% commissions; scam kiosks run 30–50%; (5) refuse 'my cousin's special tour' / 'private farm' / 'special cloud-forest access not on the website' pitches — every legitimate Monteverde operator has a TripAdvisor/Viator/GetYourGuide listing; (6) for night walks, accept the 'semi-set-up' reality (some operators habituate animals) but stick to vetted operators — Monteverde Travel, Don Juan Tours Monteverde, Wildlife Refuge Monteverde, Selvatura Night Tour.

scams.name: Monteverde Jeep-Boat-Jeep Double-Booking & Wrong-Hotel Pickup (Monteverde End)
scams.description:
The Monteverde↔Arenal (La Fortuna) jeep-boat-jeep transfer is Costa Rica's most elegant travel route — 4 hours via 4x4 from Santa Elena down to Lake Arenal, a boat across, then 4x4 up to La Fortuna — priced cheap ($22–$32/person) because multiple operators share the boat. That shared-boat economics is what makes the scam work. Community reports list the legitimate rate card: Adventuras El Lago $25, Monteverde Costa Rica $22, Desafío Costa Rica $32 — all for the same Lake Arenal crossing. One traveler noted: 'Yes jeep boat jeep. Take the am trip for less chance of rain.' Another confirmed: 'I took it today. $27 USD, 4 hours.' The Monteverde-end scams: (1) Wrong-hotel pickup — Santa Elena has 40+ hotels with similar names (Hotel Heliconia, Hotel Montañita, Cabinas Heliconia, Hotel Belmar, Hotel Belmar Sunset), the jeep arrives at the wrong one and refuses to wait, stranding the traveler; (2) Double-booked seats — operator oversells; last-arrivals told 'catch the afternoon boat' (4-hour wait) or 'refund later' (they don't); (3) Route-switch — 'jeep-boat-jeep' runs as a 6-hour van-only ride around Lake Arenal (boat leg canceled 'due to weather') with no partial refund; (4) Cash-only deposit at the last Santa Elena kiosk — strip-walking tourists are sold at $45/person ('today only') when direct is $22–$32. Monteverde-end pickup glitches hit the same Bookaway/Monteverde Shuttle Bus Company risks as the separate shuttle scam.

For travelers leaving Monteverde for La Fortuna in 2025/2026, the playbook: (1) book direct with Desafío Costa Rica ($32, desafiocostarica.com — community-favored, TripAdvisor 4.6), Adventuras El Lago ($25), or Sinwa Tours (TripAdvisor 4.5+) — pay by credit card on their own website, not at a Santa Elena kiosk; (2) confirm pickup 24h ahead via WhatsApp: exact hotel name (Hotel Belmar ≠ Hotel Heliconia ≠ Hotel Montañita), Google Maps pin, and entrance photo; (3) take the morning departure (7:30–8:00 AM) — lower weather-cancellation risk per traveler advice; (4) if boat leg is canceled day-of, demand partial refund ($10–$15) in writing before agreeing to the 6-hour van route; (5) 2025/2026 price sanity: $22–$32 direct, anything $40+ at a kiosk is a 30%+ markup — refuse; (6) for reliable pickup, stay at operator-serviced hotels (Hotel Belmar, Senda Monteverde, Hidden Canopy, Monteverde Lodge) — ask the hotel 'does Desafío/El Lago pick up here' at booking; if your hotel isn't on the list, meet at the Santa Elena soccer field / church plaza — confirm in writing.
scams.avoidance: Book direct: desafiocostarica.com ($32), Adventuras El Lago ($25), Sinwa Tours (4.5+). 24h WhatsApp confirm: exact hotel name + Maps pin + entrance photo. Take 7:30–8:00 AM departure (lower weather cancellation risk). Price sanity: $22–$32 direct, refuse kiosk rates of $40+. Stay at operator-serviced hotel (Belmar, Senda, Hidden Canopy, Monteverde Lodge).

scams.name: 'Guachimán' Yellow-Vest Watchmen Parking Extortion on the Tamarindo Strip

Variant B is the canonical TripAdvisor case 'Beware predatory surf instructor William — San Jose, Costa Rica': an instructor 'William' gave one traveler a board that was too small, steered them onto rocks at Langosta, then produced pre-existing scratches 'noticed' on the fins and pointed to the contract — $200 'damage fee.' scams.name: Rental-Car Relay-Theft & Main-Strip Smash-and-Grab outside Witch's Rock / Volcano Brewing
scams.description:
A January 2025 community post (187 upvotes) is the anchor case and the first widely-surfaced account of RFID relay theft in Costa Rica. One traveler and his wife — final lunch at Volcano Brewing/Witch's Rock Surf Camp in Tamarindo before their flight — parked 150 ft from their table on the main street, locked. Twenty minutes later their camera bag was emptied of $14,000 in pro camera gear + laptop + headphones — all neatly closed up again, bags untouched. Staff and police told them: RELAY THEFT. A thief with a signal-amplifier walks within 10 m of your table to capture the car's key-fob signal and relays it to an accomplice at the car who opens the keyless-entry locks without tripping the alarm. A Tile tracker in the camera bag was also stolen — these crews know exactly what they're looking for. One traveler (259 upvotes) wrote: 'Never leave anything in your car, ever.' Another: 'En el carro nunca.' A third cautioned: 'plenty of warnings… whether it's a touristy area or not.' The lower-tech smash-and-grab pattern runs alongside: a June 2025 community post documented a son's Beats stolen; one commenter: 'thefts of belongings in cars is probably one of the more common crimes… thieves wait and watch'; another: 'Tico Times reported 2 girls went into a gas station and came back to their car and everything was gone — just takes a minute or two while the owner is distracted.' Multiple 2024 and 2025 community traveler threads — including the widely-shared May 2024 'Tamarindo Watchmen' post (305 upvotes) — corroborate: the 'watchman' crew and the smash-and-grab crew often share the same ecosystem.

For travelers in 2025/2026: (1) EVERYTHING of value goes in the hotel/villa safe — not the trunk, not 'hidden'; never leave cameras, laptops, passports, AirTag/Tile, wallets, or designer sunglasses in a rental car; (2) buy a Faraday key-fob pouch ($10 Amazon) BEFORE the trip — blocks the key-fob relay signal; put the fob inside when you sit down at Volcano Brewing; (3) use the key's physical-button unlock, NOT proximity — disables relay attack; (4) prefer paid/staffed lots (Plaza Tamarindo underground $5, Cala Luna, Calle Central Main Lot) over unpaved main-strip shoulder; (5) take a daypack into every restaurant, beach, and surf break — dry-bag-in-the-water rule applies; (6) if hit: file OIJ 800-8000-645 + Tamarindo Fuerza Pública within 24h — required for travel insurance (Amex Platinum, Chase Sapphire Reserve, Capital One Venture X all cover rental-car theft with a filed report).
scams.avoidance: NEVER leave valuables in the car — hotel safe only; treat every parking spot as compromised. Use a Faraday key-fob pouch ($10) + physical-button unlock instead of proximity unlock. Park in staffed paid lots (Plaza Tamarindo, Cala Luna, Diria) not main-strip shoulder pullouts. Waterproof dry-bag in the water with passport/phone/cash every surf; daypack into restaurants. If hit: file OIJ 800-8000-645 + Fuerza Pública within 24h for Amex/Chase/CapOne insurance.

scams.name: Tamarindo Banco Nacional / BAC ATM Skimming + Counterfeit-Bill Swap
scams.description:
A 2024 archived community thread documents the Tamarindo-specific skimming hit: 'This happened to me as well a couple of weeks ago at the Banco Nacional in Tamarindo… Better to use the BAC ATM machines.' A parallel 2024 'Lost business visa in Tamarindo, Guanacaste Province ATM' thread anchors card-eating and retention fraud at the same ATM cluster. An April 2025 community post warns older expats to 'use BAC or BCR only, never Banco Nacional' and pull colones to avoid the DCC (dynamic-currency-conversion) upcharge. Three scams run: (1) card-skimming overlays on standalone strip-side ATMs — card data + PIN captured, cloned within days; (2) 'ATM ate my card' — device-level retention brackets prevent return, helpful 'stranger' observes your PIN re-entry; (3) the restaurant-adjacent counterfeit-bill swap, where change includes a torn or copied ₡10,000 or ₡20,000 note. A 2025 community traveler (10 upvotes) advises: 'pay in colones (and beware of the "this bill is counterfeit" scam)' — driver swaps your real ₡20,000 for a pre-palmed counterfeit. Tamarindo beach-restaurant variant: tourist hands real USD $100; waiter returns saying bill is 'torn or marked' and demands a replacement. CR banks and shops DO legally refuse damaged US notes — but the quick-switch uses that real rule to swap your good bill for a genuinely torn one.

For travelers in 2025/2026: (1) withdraw cash only INSIDE a bank branch during business hours — Scotiabank, BAC Credomatic, BCR, or Banco Nacional lobby — not from standalone curb units; branches have guards and tamper-checked machines; (2) withdraw COLONES not USD — the USD option at ATMs runs DCC ~5–9% worse; max legal foreign withdrawal is ₡400,000/day (~$770); (3) pull ₡10,000 and ₡20,000 notes for daily spend — removes counterfeit-USD-swap exposure; (4) inspect every colón note handed back — legit ₡20,000 has a Carlos Luis Fallas Sibaja watermark and color-shifting thread; counterfeits feel plastic-smooth; (5) use a no-FTF credit card (Capital One Venture, Chase Sapphire, Amex Platinum) for restaurants and hotels, colones cash only for vendors and tips; (6) if you bring USD, bring only pristine post-2013 bills (CR banks reject torn/marked/pre-2013 notes by law); (7) if skimmed: freeze the card within 30 minutes, file at Tamarindo Fuerza Pública + OIJ 800-8000-645, save the ATM receipt as chargeback evidence.
scams.avoidance: Use ATMs INSIDE bank branches during business hours (Scotiabank, BAC, BCR) — avoid curb units. Always withdraw colones not USD — decline DCC; saves 5–9% on every pull. Inspect every ₡20,000 note for Carlos Luis Fallas watermark + color-shift thread. Bring only pristine post-2013 USD bills; carry a credit card (Capital One, Chase, Amex) for restaurants. If skimmed: call bank within 30 min, file at Tamarindo Fuerza Pública + OIJ 800-8000-645.

scams.name: Fake Uber at SJO + Driver-Doesn't-End-Trip Fare Gouge
scams.description:
Uber operates in Costa Rica (since 2015) but has never been formally legalized — the ARESEP transport regulator still officially considers rideshare illegal, and airport-taxi concessionaires actively police it at SJO. This grey zone creates two scam surfaces. First, the 'fake Uber' — a pirate-taxi driver stands at arrivals with a sign showing the rider's name (pulled from a social-media leak), and peels the tourist off the real Uber. October 2025 and 2026 community reports both document the 'driver cancels, friend-cousin-with-a-van steps in' pattern. Second, the 'driver doesn't end the fare' gouge: a February 2024 community report shows a traveler paid ₡3,900 quoted, driver dropped them at SJO, sped off WITHOUT ending the ride, drove loops, ended at ₡20,000 — a 5x gouge. Another commenter advised: 'Threaten Uber with a chargeback. Your credit card company will easily refund that.' One traveler reports an Arenal surge version — quoted ₡2,300, ended ₡9,800. Another in Liberia: '$9 ride → $30 charge, over 16 km beyond actual drop-off,' refunded only after credit-card dispute. Third, the 'express kidnapping' tail: an October 2025 community report documents a driver who exited at drop-off, physically restrained the traveler, went through their pockets, took $130 cash. A 2020 community report sums the Tico view: 'At the airport take the orange taxis and everywhere else, just use Uber.' Another traveler: 'A friend paid about $200 for a ride because of a fraudulent driver (Uber refunded it).'

For travelers in 2025/2026: (1) when booking Uber at SJO meet the driver on the UPPER/DEPARTURES level (travelers advise: 'find stairs up to go to departures, and the Uber will pick you up there') — airport police enforce against Uber at arrivals but not departures; (2) VERIFY the in-app plate matches the physical plate exactly; (3) ask the driver 'cuál es mi nombre?' — if they can't name you, it's a fake Uber; (4) at drop-off DO NOT EXIT until the driver taps 'End trip' and the receipt email arrives — if they speed off, screenshot the open trip and call Uber support immediately; (5) screenshot the quoted fare before the ride starts — proof for Uber and credit-card chargeback (Capital One, Chase Sapphire, Amex Platinum handle this well); (6) prefer DiDi (travelers note: 'same software, operates throughout Latin America') or InDrive as cheaper gray-legal alternatives; (7) late-night solo travelers should prefer orange taxi or hotel shuttle over Uber at that hour — most respondents on a 2024 community thread flagged the 1 AM SJO airport Uber experience as risk-heavy.
scams.avoidance: Meet Uber on the SJO DEPARTURES level (upstairs) not arrivals — escapes airport-police ban. Verify in-app plate MATCHES physical plate + ask 'cuál es mi nombre?' before entering. Watch driver 'End Trip' in the app + receipt email arrive before exiting the vehicle. Screenshot quoted fare + route in app; dispute overages with Uber + credit-card chargeback. Prefer DiDi or InDrive at equivalent prices; late-night solo: orange taxi or hotel shuttle.
scams.location: SJO arrivals curb, the departures-level Uber pickup stairs (the workaround to the airport-police ban), the Selina/Adventure Hostel pickup zone along Avenida 7 in San José Centro, and stops near Parque Morazán where Uber drivers canceling is common

scams.name: Claro / Kolbi SIM-Card 'Activation Fee' Fraud at SJO Baggage Claim
scams.description:
A May 2023 community report captures the canonical write-up: 'Whatever you do, do NOT buy a local simcard at the Claro stand where you collect your bags in SJO airport. These guys are a fraud. They only accept cash and do not give change. They cannot give a receipt. They offer Claro's MOST EXPENSIVE pre-paid card as the "cheapest" pre-paid plan they have. The simcard you receive works for a couple of hours after which it gets blocked.' Follow-up: 'When we went to a Claro shop in San Jose the next day they told us the sim cards were not activated and thus we paid for nothing… and we needed to pay again.' One commenter noted a legit counter-example; the original traveler clarified: 'Presumably the Claro shop employees do really sell the genuine thing… but from time to time they freeload on ignorant tourists like myself and keep the money for themselves.' Mechanics: real Claro/Kolbi prepaid SIMs with 5GB run ~₡5,000–₡10,000 (~$10–$20) at any in-city Claro or Kolbi store; the airport kiosk charges $25–$45 CASH ONLY, no receipt, sells an 'activated' SIM that dies after 2 hours, pockets the difference. A parallel TripAdvisor thread 'Scammed in Tamarindo Purchasing a SIM card' documents the same vendor network at beach kiosks. Legitimate 2025/2026 alternatives: Airalo eSIM (bought before flight, activates on landing, $4.50–$17 for 1–10GB, runs on Liberty/Claro); Kolbi SIM at Multiplaza Escazú, Mall San Pedro, or a Walmart phone counter; Liberty SIM at Liberty stores ($10–$12, 4GB). One traveler noted: 'In front of the airport you can find a Walmart… you can buy a sim card for $1.' Another describes a genuine Claro activation at a legit reseller — multiple photos of passport + arrival stamp, slow but legit, ₡10,000 for 2 SIMs.

For travelers in 2025/2026: (1) BEFORE your flight install Airalo ($4.50–$9 for 1–3GB/week or $17 for 10GB/30 days at airalo.com) — activates instantly on landing, eliminates the airport-kiosk trap; (2) alternatives: Holafly, Nomad, Maya Mobile — all eSIMs work on Liberty/Claro/Kolbi networks; (3) if your phone isn't eSIM-capable, SKIP the SJO Claro kiosk — the real Kolbi store at Multiplaza Escazú (15-min Uber) or any in-city Walmart's in-store phone counter sells a legit ₡5,000–₡10,000 SIM with proper registration; (4) if you must use the airport kiosk: INSIST on a printed receipt (required under Costa Rica Ley 7472); PAY BY CARD (Claro officially accepts Visa/Mastercard; cash-only is the scam signal); test the SIM with a WhatsApp message before leaving; (5) if scammed: screenshot the transaction; file at consumidor.go.cr (Ley 7472 violation) + SUTEL telecom regulator + credit-card chargeback; (6) SJO offers free Wi-Fi ('Free-Wifi-AeropuertoSJO') — you can coordinate your Uber/shuttle without buying a SIM at all.
scams.avoidance: Pre-install Airalo eSIM ($4.50–$17) BEFORE flight — skips the airport kiosk entirely. If SIM is required: wait and buy at Multiplaza Escazú Kolbi store or Walmart phone counter. At airport kiosk: demand printed receipt + pay only by Visa/Mastercard. Test SIM with WhatsApp message before leaving the kiosk — catches dead SIMs immediately. If scammed: file at consumidor.go.cr + SUTEL + credit-card chargeback (Ley 7472).
scams.location: Kiosk at SJO baggage-claim hall 1 (between the two carousels), the arrivals-area Claro counter opposite the currency-exchange booth, and the secondary Kolbi kiosk at departures pre-security

scams.name: SJO Rental-Car Counter 'Mandatory Insurance' $2,000 Ambush — Expedia / Hertz / Fox Trap
scams.description:
This is the single highest-volume complaint in Costa Rica travel communities 2024–2026. A March 2025 community report: the traveler bought 'FULL coverage insurance from Expedia' and paid ~$1,000 for 3 weeks; on arrival at the offsite lot was told either accept a $2,032 mandatory local insurance OR pay a $32,000 USD deposit with 20% deducted for any damage; when the traveler refused they were 'left on the side of the road with 5 suitcases.' A top reply: 'Adobe and Vamos come out on top every time, and warnings about not booking through third party sites like Expedia.' Another: 'Even had this happen with Hertz.' Another: 'Same situation with me and Expedia and Fox Rental. Would not accept the Expedia insurance.' A November 2025 community report surfaces the legal reality, confirmed by another commenter: 'The law says the only required insurance is third-party liability (SLI/TPL)… NOT REQUIRED is any collision damage coverage.' TPL in 2025/2026 runs ~$13–$20/day — anything above is optional. The scam runs two ways: (1) Expedia/Priceline/Kayak's advertised $19/day balloons at the counter with $25–$40/day mandatory insurance + $2,000 deposit hold — third-party CDWs routinely rejected; (2) Hertz/Fox/Budget/National SJO counters stack 'Super CDW' to push $29/day to $90/day. Another traveler: 'If you decline CDW, you're required to bring proof of insurance from your credit card… don't forget the deposit — $2,000 for most rental companies.' Another: 'Vamos and Adobe seem to be much more straightforward about using rental insurance from a credit card.' Another: '$700 for 10 day rental with Adobe including all insurance — they were amazing.'

For travelers 2025/2026: (1) DO NOT BOOK via Expedia, Priceline, Kayak, Hotwire, Travelocity — book DIRECT with Adobe (adobecar.com), Vamos (vamosrentacar.com), or Wildrider; online quotes include TPL and are transparent; (2) if using Hertz/Budget/National, email the CR counter for an all-in written quote before landing, and bring your credit-card's rental-coverage letter (Amex Premium, Chase Sapphire Reserve Primary, Capital One Venture X Primary) on bank letterhead — required to decline CDW legally; (3) CR requires TPL (~$13–$20/day) — accept it; above is optional unless your card doesn't cover CR (most do); (4) expect $1,500–$3,000 deposit hold clearing 7–14 days post-return; (5) PHOTOGRAPH every panel on pickup + return (video walk-around) — 'pre-existing damage' counter-scam runs often; (6) Adobe, Vamos, Alamo have ZERO counter-shakedowns reported 2024–2026; Hertz/Fox/Budget/Expedia have the worst profile; (7) file disputes at consumidor.go.cr + Amex/Visa chargeback.
scams.avoidance: Book DIRECT with Adobe, Vamos, or Wildrider — published all-in pricing, honored at counter. If using Hertz/Budget/National: email counter for written quote including TPL before landing. Bring printed credit-card CDW coverage letter (Amex Premium, Chase Sapphire Reserve Primary). Accept mandatory TPL only (~$13–$20/day) — decline CDW/Super CDW with written proof. Video walk-around on pickup + return; dispute via consumidor.go.cr + chargeback if ambushed.
scams.location: SJO airport rental-car shuttle zone (arrivals → van shuttle to off-airport lots); Adobe, Vamos, Economy, Alamo, Hertz, Fox, Budget, Enterprise, National, Sixt counters clustered on the service road along Route 1 just west of the terminal

scams.name: San José Airbnb / Rental Home-Invasion — The Calendar-Leak Pattern
scams.description:
The US Embassy San José's Nov 25, 2025 Security Alert explicitly cited 'break-ins and armed robberies at vacation rentals' targeting foreign tourists. OIJ data in NY Post (Dec 2, 2025) and Tico Times (Nov 26, 2025) shows over 6,300 crimes reported against tourists in 2024 alone. An October 2025 community report is the top anchor — a family was held at gunpoint for 30 minutes at a Guanacaste Airbnb, 911 called, police arrived, gunfight erupted, one robber killed on the porch, two escaped; the traveler wrote: 'They kept asking for the cocaine which was weird because we didn't have any. They had scoped out the house prior for sure.' Confirmed by another commenter with a Teletica news link. Another: 'There's been a spree of robberies at Airbnb's over the past year or two.' Another: 'a gang of thugs who have been terrorizing the area for months.' Another traveler confirms a December Uvita Airbnb hit. Another details a Guanacaste home invasion where a tied-up couple endured a sexual assault 'she wasn't right to this day.' A 5-year Tamarindo expat: 'We were robbed by the staff at first place we stayed while we were sleeping.' An August 2025 community report on an attempted robbery on honeymoon: Playa Negra VRBO, 5–6 flashlights, alarm tripped, pile-furniture-in-bathroom defense — Vrbo refused refund. A 2025 community thread anchors the host-inside-job variant. Mechanics: Airbnb/VRBO public calendars telegraph arrival dates; scouts match addresses via Google Street View; 4–6-man gangs with handguns hit 9 PM–2 AM; isolated or weakly-gated homes in Escazú, Barrio Escalante, Santa Ana are high-profile targets. The US Embassy tells travelers: 'stay only at properties with continuous 24-hour professional security.' Canadian tourism fell 14% in H2 2025 (ticotimes.net, Dec 2025).

For travelers in San José 2025/2026: (1) book ONLY hotels with 24-hour armed guards — Hotel Grano de Oro (Barrio Amón), Intercontinental Real Costa Rica (Escazú), Hyatt Place San José, Marriott Hacienda Belén (near SJO), Hampton Inn SJO — all have verified 24/7 staff + CCTV; (2) if Airbnb, book ONLY inside a guarded gated community — Escazú porter-desk condos (Avenida Escazú, Distrito 4), Santa Ana's Río Oro or Forum Tower residences; (3) verify pre-booking in writing: '24/7 armed guard? CCTV? panic button? guard-walk log?' — 'yes to all four' is the minimum bar; (4) calendar-block ±2 days on the host's public calendar; (5) never geo-tag the property on social media; (6) program 911, OIJ 800-8000-645, US Embassy 2519-2000 into speed dial on landing; (7) if invaded: hide, call 911, comply — OIJ confirms resistance correlates with shooting; file at Fuerza Pública + OIJ within 24h.

If invaded: hide, 911, comply; file Fuerza Pública + OIJ within 24h for refund claim.

scams.name: Coca-Cola Bus Terminal Pickpocket & Luggage-Theft at the Zona Roja Edge
scams.description:
Every Western government advisory flags one zone of San José specifically: the Coca-Cola bus terminal and the 'zona roja' north of the Mercado Central. Canada's travel advisory (travel.gc.ca, 2025): 'Specific trouble spots include downtown San José areas near the Coca-Cola bus terminal, central market, and public parks.' Australia's Smartraveller: 'petty crime is common near the central bus terminal in the Coca Cola… most likely on weekends.' The zone is dense, unlit, and the hub for nearly every long-distance bus (Tracopa SJO→Jacó/Quepos; Alfaro SJO→Montezuma; MEPE SJO→Puerto Viejo; Empresarios Unidos SJO→Puntarenas). Pickpocket and luggage-lift crews work in 2–4-person cells — classic pattern: one person collides at the bus doorway, another lifts your daypack from the overhead rack, a third melts into the crowd. A canonical Tracopa-bus case, documented in a March 2024 community thread, describes how thieves planted as passengers wait for a rest stop, strip the bus of laptops/phones/passports from overhead bins, and vanish into a waiting car; one female passenger lost her laptop. A commenter's concise rule is 'take anything and everything with you if you want it when you return.' An October 2024 community thread collects the urban variants: 'Watch out for motorcyclists who can drive by and snatch a phone from your hand, or a necklace from your neck.' Another community thread warns: 'Plaza de la Cultura is safe during DAYLIGHT — pickpockets work the crowd.' Adjacent 'helpful stranger' scams: 'bird poop' on your shirt (sprayed by accomplice) + tissue + wallet lift; 'money on the ground' + two strangers claim it + your wallet vanishes during mediation.

For travelers 2025/2026: (1) AVOID Coca-Cola if possible — use Interbus (interbusonline.com) or Gray Line private shuttles ($49–$65 pp door-to-door, no terminal); (2) if using Tracopa/Alfaro/MEPE, arrive 15 minutes max ahead, stay inside the ticket office with bags on your lap, never accept 'help' with luggage from anyone not in company uniform; (3) SKIP Mercado Central and zona roja blocks north of Hotel Del Rey after dark; (4) on long-distance buses, never leave valuables in the overhead rack at a rest stop — daypack WITH you every time; (5) money belt for passport + 80% cash; decoy wallet in front pocket with expired card + ₡5,000; (6) phone on wrist-strap or zipped crossbody (Pacsafe); motorcycle-grab-from-stoplight is documented; (7) report at the Tourist Police Operations Center (San José hub opened 2025, English line) or OIJ 800-8000-645 within 24h.
scams.avoidance: Skip Coca-Cola: book Interbus/Gray Line private shuttle ($49–$65 pp, door-to-door). Never leave valuables in overhead bin during bus rest stops — carry daypack every time. Money belt under clothing for passport + 80% cash; decoy wallet in front pocket. Avoid Mercado Central / zona roja after dark; daylight only, nothing valuable in pockets. Tourist Police 24/7 hub (2025) + OIJ 800-8000-645 within 24h for insurance claim.
scams.location: Terminal 7-10 (Coca-Cola) and adjacent bus bays along Calle 14 / Avenida 1–5 in San José Centro; the Mercado Central five blocks south; the 'zona roja' (red-light) blocks immediately north of the terminal near Hotel Del Rey; nearby Tracopa, Alfaro, and MEPE bus bays

scams.name: Parque Central / Avenida 2 Cambista Currency-Exchange & 'Counterfeit Bill' Swap
scams.description:
Costa Rica has official casas de cambio and banks with BCCR (Banco Central de Costa Rica) rates ~₡515–₡530 per USD through 2025/2026 (~2% buy/sell spread). In Parque Central, Avenida 2 pedestrian strip, and around Plaza de la Cultura, informal cambistas (money-changers) approach tourists with whispered 'cambio, cambio?' and a fan of colones. Three scams run. First, the rate gouge — the quoted rate is 10–20% below market (₡450 per USD) and the cambista talks fast to close before the tourist pulls out xe.com. Second, the counterfeit-bill swap — the cambista takes your $100 USD, fans out ₡50,000 in real colones, palms one ₡20,000 out during the count and replaces it with a crisp counterfeit that feels plastic-smooth. A 2024 community report documents 'two dudes tried to scam me in San José' with a 'cambio del falso premio de lotería y otros timos callejeros' — the classic fake-lottery-prize + money-switch combo. Third, the snatch-and-run — the cambista 'counts,' feigns a mistake, asks for the dollars back, hands them to an accomplice instead of the tourist, and both vanish. Tico Times 'Costa Rica Expat Living: My Encounter with Money Changers' (June 2023) describes the pattern explicitly. A 2025 community traveler advises: 'pay in colones (and beware of the "this bill is counterfeit" scam)' — drivers claim the ₡20,000 you handed is fake, pocket yours, hand back a prepared counterfeit, demand replacement. Another 2024 community traveler: 'Biggest scam is exchanging your money at the airport. The conversion rate is terrible. Just go to a major bank.' BCCR ATMs and Banco Nacional / BAC / Scotiabank / BCR branches post rates within 1% of market.

For travelers in 2025/2026: (1) NEVER change money on the street — every whispered 'cambio' approach is a scam; (2) change at a bank branch with your passport, or withdraw colones from an in-branch ATM at a 1% spread; (3) pay shops, restaurants, taxis in COLONES not USD — removes the 'rounding' gouge; (4) check every ₡20,000 note: Carlos Luis Fallas watermark, a color-shifting security thread that flips green/blue when tilted, raised-print feel — counterfeits are smooth, lack the thread, don't flip colors; (5) if a cambista or driver claims your ₡20,000 is 'fake,' refuse to take it back and demand YOUR ORIGINAL visible in their hand — photograph it and call 911; the swap IS the scam; (6) use a no-FTF credit card (Capital One Venture, Chase Sapphire, Amex Platinum) for hotel + restaurants; colones cash only for taxis, tips, vendors; (7) BCCR ATM foreign-card limit ₡400,000/day (~$770); keep 3+ days of cash; (8) report at the San José Tourist Police Operations Center (2025) or OIJ 800-8000-645.
scams.avoidance: Never change money on the street — only bank branches or in-branch ATMs. Check ₡20,000 for Carlos Luis Fallas watermark + color-shift security thread. Refuse 'your bill is counterfeit' swap — keep YOUR original note visible + photograph it. Pay shops/taxis in COLONES (not USD) — removes the rounding-up gouge. Credit card (no-FTF Capital One/Chase/Amex) for hotels/restaurants; report at OIJ 800-8000-645.
scams.location: Parque Central San José (Avenida 2, Calle Central), Plaza de la Cultura edges, Avenida Central pedestrian strip between Calle 2 and Calle 9, the Correos de Costa Rica building cluster on Calle 2, and the casa de cambio clusters near Hotel Del Rey
